strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in autonomous driving: the computational burden of training large trajectory prediction models and the severe class/difficulty imbalance between sparse and dense traffic scenes.

The empirical investigation into scenario difficulty (stratified by traffic density/number of agents) provides useful insights into how dataset composition impacts model performance on complex multi-agent interactions.
Evaluates cross-architecture transferability by using coresets selected via HiVT-64 to train HiVT-128 and HPNet, demonstrating that data subset selection can generalize across different predictors.
weaknesses: Mathematical formulation errors and unsubstantiated claims of submodularity: In Eq. (1), the objective is written as $P(S^j) = \sum_{S^i \in \mathcal{C}} |f(S^i) - f(S^j)|^2 - \sum_{S^i \in \mathcal{D} \setminus \mathcal{C}} |f(S^i) - f(S^j)|^2$, which computes squared differences rather than similarity, conflicting directly with the text's stated goal of measuring similarity to $\mathcal{C}$. Furthermore, Algorithm 1 treats $P$ as a set function $\Delta(S^j | \mathcal{C}) = P(\mathcal{C} \cup \{S^j\}) - P(\mathcal{C})$, whereas Eq. (1) defines $P(S^j)$ as a sample-level value. No proof or formal verification of submodularity or monotonicity is provided.

Representation bottleneck: $f(S)$ is defined solely as the scalar loss output (Laplace NLL + Soft CE) of HiVT-64. Reducing high-dimensional spatio-temporal trajectories and HD map features to a single 1D scalar loss ignores scene geometry and kinematics, causing vastly different driving scenarios to appear identical if they produce similar loss values.

Insufficient baselines: The proposed method is compared solely against naive uniform random sampling. Standard data pruning, active learning, and coreset baselines (such as Facility Location, CRAIG, GradMatch, Moderate-DS, or loss-stratified sampling) are entirely absent.

Omitted selection overhead: The pipeline requires pretraining HiVT-64 on the entire dataset for 10 epochs, computing losses across all 200k+ samples, and running greedy subset iterations. The paper does not report the end-to-end wall-clock time or GPU hours for this selection phase, leaving it unclear whether the pipeline saves computation overall compared to standard training.

Limited evaluation scope: Experiments are conducted exclusively on the older Argoverse 1.1 dataset. Validation on modern, large-scale benchmarks such as Argoverse 2, Waymo Open Motion Dataset (WOMD), or nuScenes is needed to substantiate generalizability.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem: Trajectory forecasting datasets are heavily skewed toward routine, low-density traffic, leading models to underperform in safety-critical, dense multi-agent interactions. Focusing on difficulty-balanced coreset selection addresses a genuine challenge in autonomous driving.

Comprehensive exploration across keep ratios: The experimental setup thoroughly analyzes performance across retention ratios from 1% to 50% and stratifies evaluation by scene complexity (e.g., >40, >60, >80 agents).
Cross-model transferability: Coresets extracted using HiVT-64 are evaluated on HiVT-128 and HPNet, indicating reasonable architectural transferability.
weaknesses: Mathematical formulation errors and ambiguities: Equation (1) defines $P(S^j)$ on individual samples, but Algorithm 1 relies on the marginal gain $\Delta(S^j | \mathcal{C}) = P(\mathcal{C} \cup \{S^j\}) - P(\mathcal{C})$, where the set function $P(\mathcal{C})$ is never formally defined nor proved to be submodular. Furthermore, the text claims $|f(S^i) - f(S^j)|^2$ measures 'similarity', whereas squared difference is a metric of dissimilarity/distance. Moreover, since $f(\cdot)$ is the scalar training loss, selecting samples solely by 1D loss differences is fundamentally ill-suited for representing structural trajectory diversity, as radically different agent-map configurations often yield identical loss values.

Contradiction in computational efficiency claims: The core motivation is alleviating the heavy computation of training on large datasets. However, Section IV-B and V-B state that the pipeline requires pretraining HiVT-64 on the full dataset for 10 epochs and computing loss evaluations over the full dataset to construct the coreset. The paper does not report total selection runtime or wall-clock computational overhead, making it questionable whether real computational savings are achieved compared to standard training.

Absence of established data selection baselines: The proposed method is solely compared against random sampling. To substantiate the claimed contribution, it should be benchmarked against standard coreset and dataset pruning techniques (e.g., CRAIG, GradMatch, GLISTER, feature-based Facility Location, or loss-gradient based pruning).

Limited evaluation breadth: Experiments are conducted exclusively on the older Argoverse 1.1 dataset. Validation on larger and modern motion forecasting benchmarks (such as Argoverse 2, Waymo Open Motion Dataset, or nuScenes) is missing.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical challenge in autonomous driving: mitigating the computational cost of training trajectory prediction models while handling the severe class/scenario imbalance between simple and dense traffic conditions.
The intuition of explicitly partitioning data into difficulty tiers based on traffic density and rebalancing the selection budget across tiers is sensible.

Evaluates the generalization of the selected coreset across multiple model architectures (HiVT-64, HiVT-128, and HPNet) and evaluates breakdown performance on higher-density scenario subsets (>40, >60, >80 agents).
weaknesses: Mathematical formulation and submodularity claims are poorly grounded: Algorithm 1 relies on the marginal gain of a set function $\Delta(S^j \mid \mathcal{C}) = P(\mathcal{C} \cup \{S^j\}) - P(\mathcal{C})$, but Eq. (1) only defines a heuristic score $P(S^j)$ for an individual candidate rather than an underlying submodular set function $P(\mathcal{C})$. There is no proof or rigorous justification that the objective is submodular. Furthermore, reducing high-dimensional multi-agent spatio-temporal scenes to a 1D scalar loss value $f(S)$ to compute pairwise differences $|f(S_i) - f(S_j)|^2$ loses critical structural/semantic information, and the textual explanation that these terms measure 'similarity' while being maximized is conceptually contradictory.

Insufficient baseline comparisons: The only baseline evaluated across all experiments is uniform random sampling. The manuscript does not compare against established coreset and data selection techniques from the literature, such as feature-space k-Center/Facility Location, loss/uncertainty ranking, CRAIG, GradMatch, or Moderate-DS.

Missing end-to-end computational cost accounting: The central motivation of the paper is computational efficiency, yet the method requires pretraining a full HiVT-64 model for 10 epochs on the complete dataset plus computing pairwise loss comparisons across hundreds of thousands of samples. The paper does not report total wall-clock time or GPU hours incorporating selection overhead versus training directly on the full dataset.

Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (Argoverse 1.1) and relies on an overly simplistic proxy for difficulty: Scenario difficulty is determined exclusively by the raw count of agents, ignoring crucial factors such as agent speeds, trajectory curvature, high-curvature map topology, and conflict points. Validating on modern benchmarks such as Argoverse 2, nuScenes, or Waymo Open Motion is necessary to verify generalizability.

strengths: Addresses a crucial and practical bottleneck in autonomous driving research: the enormous computational cost of training trajectory prediction models on large-scale datasets and the inherent performance degradation in safety-critical, high-density scenarios due to long-tail distribution.

Solid empirical evaluation across two prominent benchmarks (Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2) and multiple representative architectures (HiVT-64, HiVT-128, HPNet, QCNet, and DeMo), demonstrating that models trained on a 50% subset can match full-dataset performance.
Shows clear and convincing improvements on challenging long-tail cases (scenes with $\ge 60$ and $\ge 80$ agents, Table 4), verifying that density-aware stratification mitigates dataset bias.

Demonstrates strong model-agnostic transferability: subsets selected using a lightweight proxy backbone (e.g., HiVT-64) generalize well when training different and more complex downstream architectures (e.g., HPNet).
weaknesses: The submodularity claims lack mathematical rigor. The manuscript describes $P(S_j)$ in Eq. (5) as a submodular gain function, but does not define the underlying set function $F(C)$ being optimized, nor does it provide a formal definition or proof of submodularity / diminishing returns.

Comparisons with existing data selection and coreset techniques are somewhat limited. While random selection, k-means, and herding are evaluated, prominent gradient-based coreset selection baselines (e.g., CRAIG, Grad-Match) discussed in related work are not compared against experimentally.

The data selection process requires pretraining a proxy model for a few epochs and performing full-dataset backpropagation to extract gradient vectors. While the authors demonstrate that this one-time cost is manageable for Argoverse, the scalability and overhead of gradient extraction on massive benchmarks (e.g., Waymo Open Motion Dataset with over 2M samples) are not thoroughly analyzed.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: trajectory prediction models require substantial computation on large-scale datasets, and the distribution across traffic scenario densities is inherently long-tailed.
The proposed density-aware partitioning combined with gradient-based subset selection is well-motivated and intuitive for trajectory forecasting.
Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple state-of-the-art architectures (HiVT-64/128, HPNet, QCNet, DeMo) on both Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2 benchmarks.

Crucial practical finding: selecting 50% data via SSTP yields performance nearly identical to full-dataset training, and notably outperforms full-dataset training on high-density agent scenarios (Agent >= 60 and >= 80).
Good cross-model transferability analysis showing that subsets extracted using one architecture (e.g., HiVT) transfer effectively to different target models (e.g., HPNet).
weaknesses: Theoretical loose ends regarding submodularity: The paper frequently refers to Eq. (5) as a 'submodular gain function' and claims submodular optimization, but does not explicitly define the underlying set function $F(C_k)$ or prove that it satisfies submodularity (diminishing marginal gains).

Missing comparisons with established gradient-based coreset selection baselines: While the authors cite relevant coreset selection works like CRAIG (Mirzasoleiman et al., 2020) and Grad-Match (Killamsetty et al., 2021), the empirical comparisons are limited to simple heuristics (Random, K-Means, Herding).

Computational savings are modest for faster backbones: For HiVT-64, total time including selection is 6.37h vs. 7.78h for full training (saving ~1.4h), although savings become substantial for heavier models like HPNet (137.1h vs. 268.8h). A clearer discussion on amortization across repeated experiments/hyperparameter tuning would clarify the real-world efficiency trade-off.
Despite using the Waymo Open Motion Dataset (WOMD) to heavily motivate the problem in the introduction, experimental validation is omitted for WOMD.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem in autonomous driving: the high computational cost of training trajectory prediction models on massive datasets, as well as the long-tail imbalance with respect to scene complexity.
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple state-of-the-art trajectory prediction architectures (HiVT-64, HiVT-128, HPNet, QCNet, DeMo) on both Argoverse 1 and Argoverse 2 benchmarks.

Demonstrates an interesting and useful empirical property: training on a density-balanced 50% subset can outperform full-dataset training on dense, safety-critical scenarios (e.g., scenes with >60 or >80 agents), mitigating long-tail performance degradation.
Thorough ablation studies analyzing the impact of backbone pretraining epochs, partitioning intervals, and transferability of selected subsets across different predictor backbones.
weaknesses: Unsubstantiated submodular optimization claims: The paper claims to employ a submodular gain function and greedy submodular optimization, but does not define an underlying set function F(S), nor does it provide proofs or citations verifying that the objective in Eq. (5) satisfies submodularity (diminishing marginal returns) or guarantees standard greedy approximation bounds.

Modest net wall-clock efficiency gains when factoring in preprocessing overhead: For HiVT, full dataset training takes 7.78 hours, while SSTP requires 2.17 hours for pretraining/extraction/selection plus 4.20 hours for training (totaling 6.37 hours), yielding only an ~18% net speedup. A more detailed breakdown of wall-clock time across each phase (pretraining, gradient backprop, greedy selection) for all models is needed to substantiate practical efficiency.

Limited coreset and sample selection baselines: Comparisons are restricted to basic heuristics (Random, K-Means, and Herding). Established gradient-based or error-based coreset selection baselines (e.g., Grad-Match, CRAIG, EL2N) are cited in related work but omitted from the experimental comparison.

Overly simplistic density proxy: Partitioning depends solely on agent count per scene, which ignores other critical factors of driving complexity such as intersection geometry, agent velocities, turning maneuvers, or static vs. dynamic vehicle distributions.

Presentation and completeness issues: The GitHub URL in the abstract is an incomplete placeholder (https://github.com/ .), and the dynamic budget allocation logic in Algorithm 1 requires clearer mathematical justification regarding how it guarantees coverage across all partitions.
